sections.h2: Which Chatham County office does what on property tax?
sections.html:
Tax Administration is split into a Listing Division, an Appraisal Division and a Collections Division. The Listing Division is at 12 East Street in Pittsboro, on the ground floor of the government annex facing the Pittsboro traffic circle. Its public counter operates on weekdays, eight to five. Mail goes to PO Box 908, Pittsboro, NC 27312, and the listing line is 919-542-8250.

Questions about what your house is worth on the tax roll go to the Appraisal Division at 919-542-8211. Bills, payments and returned-check issues go through Collections.

The county had an estimated 85,111 people in mid-2025, 11.6% more than in 2020. Pittsboro, Siler City and Goldston levy their own town taxes, and slices of Chatham near Cary and Apex are billed for those towns too. That mix is why two Chatham neighbors can have different bills on similar houses.

The county reappraises every four years, well inside the eight-year ceiling that G.S. 105-286 sets for every North Carolina county. The latest reappraisal took effect January 1, 2025, following one in 2021. If the county keeps that rhythm, the next value date lands in 2029. The Appraisal Division can confirm it.

For the 2025 round, county appraisers studied recorded sales, building cost data and income and expense figures from commercial property to estimate values for more than 48,000 parcels. Many parts of the county went up in value from 2021, a few went down and some stayed about the same.

The tax rate is a separate step, set from each taxing body's budget. Commissioners held the county rate at 60 cents per $100 of valuation for fiscal year 2026-27.

The county-only rate is 0.60, and every other district adds its own piece on top. The county rate sheet prints a district rate and a combined rate for each area, and the combined figure is the one that matches a bill.

The county budget year begins July 1, which is also when commissioners and the towns fix rates. Phone the tax office to learn which district covers your street address.

sections.h2: How to appeal a Chatham County value
sections.html:
Begin with the county's comparison tool, file with the Appraisal Division next, and take the matter to the county's equalization board only if the staff review leaves you unsatisfied. The county encourages owners to test a notice against nearby sales on its Comper website. An online appeal form lives on the appraisal page, and a printable paper form is available too.

  • Comparable sales, from your own research, the county's site or a real estate professional.
  • Photos of the inside and outside of the property, showing condition and upgrades.
  • A recent fee appraisal, such as one done for a purchase or refinance.

After an appeal is received, a tax office representative contacts the owner to go over the value. Still unresolved? Request a hearing, and the board mails its written finding. The Board of Equalization and Review sits each spring and takes no new appeals once it adjourns, so file early.

Two statutes set the outer frame. G.S. 105-322 puts the board's first sitting in April or early May, and G.S. 105-290 gives a 30-day clock for taking a loss to the Property Tax Commission.

sections.h2: Relief programs that reduce a tax bill
sections.html:
Chatham runs three state programs plus one local grant. For the state programs, the Tax Listing Office must receive your application before June 1 of the year you qualify.

  • Elderly or disabled exclusion: for residents who are 65 or older, or totally and permanently disabled, with income up to $38,800, the exclusion is the larger of $25,000 or half the home's appraised value.
  • Disabled veteran exclusion: a disabled veteran resident or unmarried surviving spouse has $45,000 taken off appraised value. The NCDVA-9 form comes from the state division that handles veteran benefits.
  • Circuit breaker deferment: tax is capped at a share of income for owners who are 65-plus or totally disabled, earn $58,200 or less, and have owned and lived in the house five calendar years. The excess stays as a lien, and the most recent three years of deferred tax are due, with interest, if a disqualifying event occurs. A new application is needed each year.
  • Low Income Tax Relief Program: a grant of up to $500, capped at 50% of the current bill, for residents who have owned and lived in the home five years and have household income at or below 60% of area median income. Food and Nutrition Services households skip the income paperwork.

A disability claim needs a certificate from a North Carolina physician or a government agency. Heirs or executors must tell the office when a recipient dies, and a surviving spouse reapplies for the following year. Failing to report a disqualifying event means recovery of the exclusion plus penalties and interest.

sections.h2: Due dates, and tax owed at closing
sections.html:
Each September 1 is the due date, and G.S. 105-360 allows payment without interest through January 5. Interest of 2% starts January 6, and from February 1 three-fourths of one percent is added for every month or fraction. A check or electronic payment that bounces draws a penalty of $25 or 10% of the payment, whichever is greater, up to $1,000.

A tax lien attaches on the listing date under G.S. 105-355, so the bill follows the house, not the seller. Usually the closing office pays the current year's tax from the seller's funds, and the buyer carries it forward. Owners who let a bill go unpaid can face a tax foreclosure sale held at the courthouse door, with the sale price applied to taxes, penalties, interest and costs under G.S. 105-374.

For 2020 to 2024 owner-occupancy was 80.6% and the median home value was $446,200. Anyone receiving a program benefit should ask the Listing Division what a sale does to it. Get the open balance from Collections and give it to your closing attorney before the contract date.

sections.h2: What recording a Chatham County deed costs
sections.html:
The seller pays the state excise tax of $1.00 per $500 of consideration at the register of deeds office, as G.S. 105-228.30 provides. Recording a deed of up to 15 pages costs $26.00 at the Chatham County Register of Deeds, plus $4.00 per added page. A deed of trust is $64 for up to 35 pages.

These recording amounts mirror the uniform schedule in G.S. 161-10. Your closing office will supply exact settlement figures, because they turn on the price and the number of pages.

faqs.q: Where do I pay or question my Chatham County property tax bill?
faqs.a: Call the Tax Administration offices in Pittsboro. The Listing Division answers at 919-542-8250 and the Appraisal Division at 919-542-8211. Payments go through Collections. The Listing Division is at 12 East Street and keeps weekday hours of 8:00 to 5:00.

faqs.q: What is the Chatham County county-only tax rate?
faqs.a: For 2026 it is 0.60, the same as the 60 cents per $100 of valuation commissioners kept for fiscal year 2026-27. Towns and fire districts add their own rates, so your full rate depends on where the parcel sits.

faqs.q: When can I appeal my Chatham County value?
faqs.a: The Board of Equalization and Review sits each spring and accepts no new appeals once it adjourns. Owners can still talk to the Appraisal Division about errors, and the next reappraisal brings a new notice and a new window.

faqs.q: Can a Chatham County senior get a lower assessment?
faqs.a: Yes, if age and income fit. Owners 65 or older with income up to $38,800 can have $25,000 or 50% of appraised value excluded, whichever is greater. File before June 1 with the Tax Listing Office.

faqs.q: Who pays the deed excise tax in Chatham County?
faqs.a: The seller does. The $1.00 per $500 charge falls on the transferor and is paid to the register of deeds before recording, usually deducted from proceeds by the closing office.
